concept.name: Cancellation rate
concept.definition: The rate or fraction at which resting orders are cancelled before execution. In automated markets the large majority of displayed orders are cancelled rather than executed - the SEC notes that high-frequency liquidity providers cancel a very high percentage of their orders, and the CFTC lists cancel-to-fill ratios among the objective measures of high message rates.
concept.intuition: Most quotes are withdrawn, not traded; the cancellation rate tells you how quickly the visible book evaporates and renews.
concept.mechanics: Computed as cancellations per unit time or as cancels relative to cancels plus executions, per participant, instrument, or venue; together with arrival rates it determines queue-position dynamics and the fill probability of resting orders.
concept.formula: Cancellation rate = N_cancels / (N_cancels + N_executions) over an interval, or cancels per second.
concept.failure_modes: When cancellation rates are extreme, displayed depth becomes a weak proxy for executable liquidity; spikes in cancellations also accompany stress episodes and manipulative quoting schemes.
concept.misconceptions: High cancellation is mostly normal risk management by market makers repricing to new information - it is not inherently evidence of spoofing or phantom liquidity.
concept.example: Of 1,000 lots a market maker posts in a minute, 950 are cancelled unfilled, a 95 percent cancellation rate typical of active electronic quoting.

citations.source: CFTC, Concept Release on Risk Controls and System Safeguards for Automated Trading Environments, 78 FR 56542
citations.section: Part II.A.1 (cancel-to-fill ratios as message-rate measures)
